_comment: Machine-readable provenance for every third-party input. Each generated
dataset names the source ids it derives from, and its licence is whatever
is compatible with all of them. See LICENSE-DATA.md for the rule.
'redistributable' is whether the bytes may be republished from here, which
is a different question from whether they may be used.
'url' is the canonical origin. Where 'via' names the Wayback Machine, the
bytes were fetched through it because census.gov refuses automated
clients: snapshots are found with the CDX index at
suppresses the Archive's own rewriting. See usa/tools/fetch_census.py.

'share_alike' true means a dataset built from this one must carry the same licence. It is the field that decides an output's terms, so it is recorded explicitly rather than inferred from the licence string.

Datasets from a Dataverse repository are cited to the standard that project defines: author, title, year, repository, version, persistent identifier, and UNF. The last two are machine-readable, and the UNF is the point -- it is a cryptographic fingerprint of the data's content, not its file format, so it identifies exactly which version was used and changes if any of it does. Citing the DOI alone names the dataset but not the version, which for a dataset revised twenty times is not enough to reproduce anything.

sources.title: Block-level election results, 2008-2024
sources.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0, with an added clause forbidding sale of the data
sources.attribution: Election data: Dave's Redistricting (CC BY-SA 4.0), from the Voting and Election Science Team (2016, 2018, 2020), Ryne Rohla / Decision Desk HQ (2012), Steve Gerontakis with John Mifflin (2008), and the Redistricting Data Hub (2024)
sources.note: Votes already disaggregated to 2020 census blocks, which is why it is used: allocating county totals by population erases the sorting inside a county and put 239 districts in Democratic hands on the enacted 2012 map where the true answer is 209. At block level that error disappears. 52 states, 614 MB. Share-alike, so any map carrying these results is CC BY-SA rather than the CC-BY the cut trees carry. DRA's own licence file names its upstreams; those are recorded in 'upstream' with full Dataverse citations, because crediting the packager alone would hide who actually collected the returns. The bytes are served from data.dra2020.net, not from the GitHub repo named in 'url'; the per-state version numbers are tracked in usa/upstream/dra_versions.json because a rebuild cannot reproduce the checksums without them. The server rejects HEAD, so probing for new versions needs a ranged GET.

sources.title: 113th Congress Block Equivalency Files
sources.note: The enacted 2012 districts expressed on 2010 census blocks, so no geometry is needed to score them. This is what let the vote pipeline be validated against a known answer rather than trusted.

sources.title: County Presidential Election Returns 2000-2024
sources.publisher: MIT Election Data and Science Lab
sources.licence: CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication), per the dataset's Dataverse record
sources.attribution: MIT Election Data and Science Lab, 2018, "County Presidential Election Returns 2000-2024", https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ, Harvard Dataverse, V20, UNF:6:xvsJJxrfXMIvzAuDYlfvVw==
sources.note: Used for the seven at-large states, whose single district is the whole state, so only the state total matters and no allocation is involved. Also a cross-check on the block data. Their Dataset Terms dialog confirms CC0 1.0 and asks, as a community norm rather than a condition, that the data citation above be used; maps drawing on it carry that credit. The file is guestbook-gated (guestbookID 458) and no API parameter bypasses it, so updating it needs a person. countypres_2000-2016.csv is the superseded copy, kept only because its codebook documents the older column names that the 2024 revision changed.

sources.title: Votacao por partido, municipio e zona (Deputado Federal), 1994-2022
sources.via: direct from cdn.tse.jus.br with a browser's Sec-Fetch-* headers; Wayback Machine as fallback
sources.licence: open government data; TSE Portal de Dados Abertos publishes these for free reuse
sources.attribution: Election data: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, Portal de Dados Abertos
sources.note: Votes by party per municipality and electoral zone, aggregated to the state, which is the district. Both nominal and legenda votes count toward a party's total under Brazilian law, so both are summed. TSE's CDN is behind Akamai: it refuses HEAD from anything and refuses GET unless the request carries a browser's full navigation header set, the Sec-Fetch-* trio in particular. 1990 is a genuine 404 under every odsele dataset name -- TSE's machine-readable repository begins in 1994. Each archive also contains _BRASIL.csv and _BR.csv aggregates that repeat every state's rows, so reading the whole archive double-counts the country; and the 1998 archive ships no DF file, that state existing only inside the aggregate. The 1994 file records zero legenda votes in every state and is therefore unusable for seat allocation. Snapshots and checksums in brazil/upstream/tse/snapshots.json.

sources.title: Populacao residente por Unidade da Federacao, censuses 1991/2000/2010/2022
sources.publisher: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatistica
sources.licence: open, IBGE/SIDRA; free reuse with attribution
sources.note: SIDRA table 136 for 1991-2010 and table 4709 for 2022; IBGE renumbers tables between censuses rather than extending one. Joined to TSE by UF numeric code, never by name. Totals match the published census figures exactly. 27 KB, so the bytes are committed.

sources.title: Election Passport, Brazil: Chamber of Deputies votes by party and state, 1982-2014
sources.author: David Lublin
sources.licence: free public access for research; terms stated on electionpassport.com
sources.attribution: Brazil constituency results: David Lublin, Election Passport (electionpassport.com)
sources.note: The only reachable source for the 1990 election, which predates TSE's machine-readable repository, and the only usable source for 1994, whose TSE file records no legenda votes. Party totals per state, not coalition totals, so it supports a party-level series rather than Brazil's actual pre-2020 rule. Carries a BRASIL row of national totals used as a checksum: the 27 states sum to it exactly in every year but 2006, which is off by 763 votes in the source. 88 KB, committed because it is small and because its upstream is a personal academic site with no archival guarantee. Election Passport is merging into the Constituency-Level Elections Archive (CLEA), which is the better long-term citation. Documentation in BR.pdf.

sources.title: Camara dos Deputados em 1990 / em 1994: seats by state and party
sources.attribution: Seat tables: Portuguese Wikipedia, 'Camara dos Deputados em 1990' and 'em 1994' (CC BY-SA 4.0)
sources.note: The historical apportionment tables, unavailable from TSE. Stored as the original wikitext and parsed by brazil/tools/parse_wikitable.py, which enforces the checks rather than reporting them: every row must sum to its published Soma and the states to the chamber size, or the table is rejected. 1990 reconciles completely, columns included. 1994's cells originally gave PMDB 106 against a published 107 and PSDB 64 against 63; the error was localised to Rio Grande do Norte, which elected two PMDB deputies and one PSDB rather than the reverse, and is corrected in the parser so re-parsing cannot undo it. Both tables now reconcile on rows, on columns and on the chamber size. The two tables differ in exactly one state: Sao Paulo, 60 against 70, so the whole ten-seat expansion of LC 78/1993 went there. The 1994 table reproduces the LC 78/1993 distribution used throughout, independently confirming it. Share-alike, but it feeds only a set of seat counts -- integers that are facts, not expression -- so the outputs stay CC-BY.

sources.title: Camara dos Deputados: plenary roll-call summaries, 2003-2024
sources.licence: open government data, Camara dos Deputados Dados Abertos
sources.attribution: Roll-call data: Camara dos Deputados, Dados Abertos
sources.note: One record per division with the tallies, 173 MB for 2003-2024; checksums in brazil/upstream/camara/manifest.json. Used to screen for votes close enough that the apportionment could have decided them, before spending the per-deputy layer (votacoesVotos-YYYY.json, 7-79 MB per year) on the shortlist. Coverage begins in 2003, so the 1990, 1994 and 1998 seat counterfactuals cannot be tested against actual votes. Two years arrived truncated on the first pass and needed re-fetching, so file sizes are worth checking against the manifest rather than trusting the download. Per-deputy positions for the 56 shortlisted divisions come from the API at /api/v2/votacoes/{id}/votos, which carries each deputy's party and state and returns a whole division in one page; that costs a few hundred kilobytes against roughly 700 MB for the bulk per-deputy files.

sources.title: Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database (HSall votes, rollcalls and members)
sources.publisher: Voteview, University of California Los Angeles
sources.licence: no licence statement published; the project asks that the dataset be cited
sources.attribution: Lewis, Jeffrey B., Keith Poole, Howard Rosenthal, Adam Boche, Aaron Rudkin and Luke Sonnet (2026). Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database. https://voteview.com/
sources.note: 737 MB across the three files, of which the House for congresses 113-117 is 5,679 roll calls and 2.4 million cast votes. 'redistributable' is false because no licence is stated, not because reuse is refused -- the data page gives only a citation request, so republishing the bytes from here would be asserting a permission nobody granted. Two traps in the files. Voteview records presidential position-taking as cast votes on House roll calls (574 of these), so counting every row overstates a tally by one; and several integer columns are written as floats ('10713.0'), which int() rejects. Excluding the President while keeping delegates and independents reproduces the published yea/nay counts on all 5,679 roll calls, which is the check that the join is right.

sources.title: Cifras Oficiales de Poblacion de los Municipios Espanoles: Revision del Padron Municipal, by province, 1996-2025
sources.licence: reuse authorised by INE for commercial and non-commercial purposes, on condition that the source is cited, the last-update date is given, the sense of the data is not distorted, and no INE endorsement is implied
sources.attribution: Elaboracion propia con datos extraidos del sitio web del INE: www.ine.es
sources.note: The padron is the population LOREG art. 162 apportions on, and it is not the resident-population series INE has published since 2021 under the Estadistica Continua de Poblacion -- a different concept with different numbers that would move seats. Two tables are needed because INE froze the province-level one: table 2852 covers 1996-2021 and stops, so later years are read off the 52 per-province municipal tables, where INE marks the province aggregate by giving it a two-digit code where a municipality has five. Code '00' in the same table is the national total and passes that filter too, so it is dropped by name. The overlap between the two sources is checked for exact agreement on every province-year before anything is written. 30 KB, so the bytes are committed.

sources.title: LOREG art. 162 and the seven royal decrees convoking general elections, 2008-2023
sources.publisher: Agencia Estatal Boletin Oficial del Estado
sources.licence: public domain as legal text (Spanish LPI art. 13 excludes legal and regulatory provisions from copyright); BOE additionally authorises reuse of its electronic-office documents under Ley 37/2007 and the licence approved by its Resolution of 27 June 2024
sources.attribution: Agencia Estatal Boletin Oficial del Estado
sources.note: Art. 162.4 requires each convoking decree to state the number of Diputados per constituency, and its annex is the only published form of the official apportionment -- nobody else publishes the seat vector. The decree ids are read out of the relevant day's BOE sumario rather than typed in, so how each was found survives with it. The annex is anchored on its two-line header 'Circunscripcion' / 'Diputados' rather than on the word ANEXO, because the 2008 decree puts the table inline in article 3 and has no annex at all; and every decree before 2023 writes the seat counts as Spanish number words. What no decree states is which padron revision it used, which is why that is found empirically rather than assumed.

outputs.note: One plan per (year, state, seats, model, metric); the model is in the filename so a file is identifiable outside its directory. Browsable views over these live in usa/maps/ and are rebuilt by tools/make_views.py rather than stored. Every input is public domain, so the licence is a choice rather than an inheritance. CC-BY rather than CC0 to keep reuse citable.

Share-alike, inherited from the election data -- not the CC-BY the cut trees carry. A map showing election results and a map showing only districts are under different licences, and each says so in its own credit line.
Per-district two-party margins for each (plan, contest) pair, plus national summaries. Share-alike, inherited from the election data.

Voting-age population by race and Hispanic origin per district, PL 94-171 table P4. Every input is public domain, so this is CC-BY rather than the CC-BY-SA the vote scorings carry -- no election data is involved.

Seats per state and per party under the actual apportionment, under the constitutional rule recomputed on current population, under a floor of 1 with no ceiling, and under a single national district, for nine Chamber elections 1990-2022. Two series because seats were won by coalitions until 2018: TSE is coalition-level (1998-2022), Election Passport party-level (1990-2014). All inputs are freely reusable with attribution and none is share-alike, so CC-BY as with the US plans.

Plenary divisions within a chosen distance of the bar that actually applied to them -- a simple majority for ordinary matters, 308 of 513 for constitutional text. Mentioning a PEC is not the same as being subject to its three-fifths bar: motions on preference, urgency and waivers of interval pass on a simple majority, and scoring those against 308 invents near-misses that never existed.

Probability that each shortlisted division would have gone the other way under an apportionment without the constitutional floor and ceiling. Delegations are resampled by state -- not by party, because 20-30% of deputies switch party mid-term and cannot be matched to the cell they were elected in -- with both sides resampled together and absences included in the draw. Exact by construction when the apportionment is unchanged.

The same scoring repeated across the model, cut-metric and house-size axes, to say how much of the headline is the finding and how much is the parameter choice. Two of the five runs are recorded as gate failures rather than results: under a larger house the seven states with no block-level election data need two districts each, the statewide shortcut that covers them stops applying, and they fall out of every plan in the run including the enacted baseline. Share-alike, inherited from the election data.

Population-weighted mean distance from a resident to their district's population-weighted centroid, per state and nationally, for the splitline and enacted 2010 plans. Olson's BDistricting objective, chosen because it is defined on block assignments rather than on shapes -- the enacted plan reaches us with no polygons, so a perimeter score cannot be computed for it. Both plans are scored on 2010 blocks, so there is no crosswalk in this path. No election data is involved, so CC-BY rather than the CC-BY-SA the vote scorings carry.

House roll calls, congresses 113-117, that are both within 25 votes of the bar that actually applied and divided by more than 50 points between the parties. The bar is not always a simple majority: suspension of the rules and veto overrides need two thirds, and a suspension motion carried 290-140 fails, so measuring those against the other side's total would fill the candidate set with comfortable losses.

Probability that each shortlisted roll call would have gone the other way under splitline districts. Unlike Brazil, the delegation is resampled at constant size: US apportionment fixes how many seats a state has, so the counterfactual converts members between parties rather than adding or removing them, drawing the arrivals from that state's observed members of the receiving party with absences included. The seat difference is applied, not the level, because 231 and 209 are districts carried by a presidential candidate while the House that sat was 201 D. Exact by construction when no seat moves. Share-alike, because the per-state deltas come from the DRA-derived scorings.

Seats per province for seven general elections 2008-2023 under LOREG art. 162 and under three counterfactuals -- the provincial floor cut from two seats to one, no floor at all, and Sainte-Lague in place of quota-and-remainders -- with the malapportionment statistics for each. Every official column reproduces the convoking decree's annex province by province, which is the gate. Neither input is share-alike, so CC-BY as with the Brazilian counterfactuals.
